transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-02-09
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 75 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Head of ML, Harborlytics), Rajiv Menon (Platform Eng), Aisha Khan (FinOps), Tom Breuer (CTO)

Auto-generated summary (may be rough):
- Purpose: kickoff a short sprint to align on cost/runway, SLA targets, and pilot scope for moving Harborlytics workloads to Redwood Dedicated/Hosted hybrid.
- Key asks: Harborlytics to share usage histograms and spend targets; Redwood to provide pilot pricing, security docs, fallback runbooks, and KV-cache/batching recommendations.
- Next steps and owners captured below.

Topics: cost runaway, committed capacity vs burst, latency SLOs, KV cache and batching, SOC2/KMS, pilot metrics and acceptance criteria.

----- Transcript -----
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll keep this tight 75 minutes ish, uh agenda is finops runway, sla targets, and then a quick tech run through with Omar for any blockers. everyone good?
[00:18] Tom Breuer: yeah all good, thanks Maya. small ask up front i'd like a clear outcome: ok to pilot, target SLAs, and cost envelope.
[00:26] Maya Chen: perfect. lena, do you want to kick off with where you are on usage and what your chief concerns are?
[00:33] Lena Ortiz: sure. so we're seeing steady growth in our chat summarization and search features, tokens per month have gone from ~40M to 120M in last quarter, but the big issue is latency spikes during afternoon ET peak. the tail latency's killing the UX. we also want to cap monthly inference spend to about $35k while we experiment with quantization and batching.
[01:02] Aisha Khan: just to add i need predictability, our finance team wants commitments, not surprise bursts. we can do a reserved plan but we need to see the math on whether dedicated capacity reduces unit cost enough to justify the commit.
[01:18] Omar Patel: yeah makes sense. there are a few levers: dedicated pools for baseline throughput, autoscale for burst, and then caching and batching to reduce per-token compute. for tail you'll want prefix caching + small hot-key reservations to keep KV cache warm.
[01:36] Rajiv Menon: can you say more about KV cache warm? our current infra evicts quickly cause we want predictability, so warm caches sound like a memory overhead.
[01:47] Omar Patel: totally. what we do is keep a small pinned pool that holds the most common conversation prefixes; that narrows fetch latency. it's a tradeoff — memory for latency. we can give you numbers: for your prompt distribution probably a couple of hundred MB of KV cache reduces 95th pct by ~30-40% on typical models. that's based on similar profiles we've seen.
[02:11] Lena Ortiz: interesting. and about quantization — we're worried about quality regressions, particularly on summarization. can Redwood help surface expected ROUGE/bleu style regressions?
[02:23] Omar Patel: yes, we'll run the pilot with a small eval set you provide. we do a delta analysis per prompt set and flag any regressions. early quant profiles reduce cost ~20-40% with small quality delta, depends on model and prompt length.
[02:36] Maya Chen: ok let's anchor success criteria: 95th pct latency under 800ms for web requests, cost reduction target 25% vs current hosted baseline, and no quality regressions on the supplied eval set beyond an agreed threshold. does that sound reasonable?
[02:56] Tom Breuer: 800ms is aggressive but doable if we commit to dedicated pools, yes.
[03:03] Aisha Khan: 25% cost reduction we'd need to see a financial model; also we may be looking for an option to step into a committed tier mid-pilot if numbers look good.
[03:11] Maya Chen: we can include a graduated commit example in the pricing doc — incremental discounts based on volume and reserved vCPU/GPU commitment.
[03:18] Rajiv Menon: on security — our auditors want SAML SSO, KMS for keys, and audit logs to ship to our SIEM. we need to confirm private deployment option compatibility.
[03:29] Maya Chen: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and can forward audit logs; SSO is supported via SAML, SCIM for provisioning — we'll attach the integration guide. we also have SOC2 and ISO summaries we'll share.
[03:40] Lena Ortiz: awesome. one operational question: when a model rollout happens and we fallback to a smaller model, how does Redwood handle semantic drift or differences in hallucination profile?
[03:52] Omar Patel: we have routing policies per route. you can set a policy to prefer a high-quality model, and a fallback to a quantized variant or smaller family. we also support canary rollouts and automatic quality checks based on your eval set — if the metric drops, the system auto-rolls back. small caveat, metrics are only as good as the prompt set.
[04:12] Maya Chen: i'll note that as an operational constraint — an eval surface needs to be part of the pilot.
[04:18] [04:18] Speaker 1: mm-hmm
[04:22] Lena Ortiz: ok on observability, can we get token-level cost breakdowns per route so our product teams can see which features drive spend?
[04:30] Omar Patel: yes — Redwood Console exposes token and route-level cost, we can also push daily CSVs to an S3 bucket if you'd like.
[04:37] Aisha Khan: can those be annotated with model version and quantization profile? we need to tie spend to quality.
[04:44] Omar Patel: yes, we'll include model tags, quant-profile, and route name in the export.
[04:49] [04:49] Maya Chen: switching to pilot scope — recommended approach is 4-week pilot: week 0 discovery and data sharing, week 1 baseline benchmarking on hosted, week 2 reserved/dedicated tuning and KV cache/batching config, week 3 stress testing and rollback/playbook validation. acceptance criteria: latency & cost targets plus regression test pass.
[05:11] Rajiv Menon: for benchmarking do you require test harness code or can we provide traces?
[05:16] Omar Patel: traces are fine; we can replay them with our bench harness or run live A/B with shaded traffic. traces give fast repeatability, A/B gives more realistic signal.
[05:26] Lena Ortiz: we'd prefer A/B but may start with trace replay to iterate faster.
[05:31] Tom Breuer: one more constraint — our network is egress-sensitive; can Private be run inside our VPC to avoid egress?
[05:39] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood Private can be deployed in your VPC or on-prem; for egress-sensitive workloads we recommend Private, or a hybrid where PII/critical routes hit Private and lower-confidence routes use Hosted.
[05:52] [05:52] Aisha Khan: cost question: how do you price the reserved GPUs versus per-token hosted? give me an example.
[05:58] Maya Chen: example: a mid-sized reserved pool with 2x A100-equivalent GPUs might be X per month (we'll detail in spreadsheet) vs hosted per-token which is Y. the math depends on utilization; if you can run at >50% utilization on reserved, you often see 30-40% unit cost savings. we will show scenarios.
[06:21] Rajiv Menon: do you have price variability for different regions? we operate multi-region and want consistent SLAs.
[06:26] Omar Patel: regional pricing differs slightly; SLOs are the same but cost can vary. we can present a regional-adjusted PV model in the pricing doc.
[06:34] [06:34] crosstalk - multiple people
[06:36] Maya Chen: question for Omar — for the afternoon tail spikes what combination of batching and KV cache tends to be most effective without increasing cold-start latency?
[06:45] Omar Patel: continuous batching helps for throughput but increases per-request latency if you wait for batch fill; adaptive batching with latency caps plus prefix KV-cache gives the best of both worlds — it batches opportunistically but also serves hot requests immediately from cache.
[06:58] Lena Ortiz: do you support per-route latency caps so we can have stricter SLOs for web endpoints and laxer for offline jobs?
[07:05] Omar Patel: yes route-level SLOs and policies exist. you can also tag routes for cost center attribution.
[07:11] Maya Chen: ok any major blockers from Harborlytics side before we prepare the pilot materials?
[07:16] Aisha Khan: audit docs and a clear financial model.
[07:20] Rajiv Menon: histogram of prompt lengths and a sample of the biggest 500 prompts.
[07:24] Lena Ortiz: a small eval set for quality checks.
[07:28] Tom Breuer: and a runbook for failover — how your system will degrade and who we call.
[07:33] Maya Chen: we'll provide a draft runbook and escalation contacts. Omar will include the technical fallback and cache tuning recommendations.
[07:40] [07:40] Omar Patel: i'll also sketch the automatic fallback policy and show how to configure canaries in the Console.
[07:47] Maya Chen: great. let's quickly talk about timeline: we aim to get pricing and docs to you by Friday 2027-02-12, Harborlytics to send usage histograms by 2027-02-16; kickoff pilot week of 2027-02-22.
[07:58] Aisha Khan: that timeline works, finance approves review once they see the model.
[08:02] Lena Ortiz: technical note — when you test quantized models please include the beam/temperature settings we use, otherwise results aren't comparable.
[08:11] Omar Patel: good call, include config file or example calls and we'll mirror those in bench.
[08:17] [08:17] Maya Chen: any questions about security posture?
[08:20] Rajiv Menon: one more: can audit logs be routed to a customer-managed S3 with KMS encryption and be retained for 90 days?
[08:29] Maya Chen: yes, retention windows are configurable; we'll note 90 days as default for pilot.
[08:33] Tom Breuer: will you provide an SLA for the dedicated pool during pilot? we need at least 99.5% uptime.
[08:40] Maya Chen: pilot will run under an interim SLA; for Dedicated we can offer contractual SLA with the reserved plan — typical enterprise plans aim for 99.9% but for pilots we commonly aim for 99.5%. we'll put options in the offer.
[08:52] [08:52] Lena Ortiz: ok i'm comfortable with next steps.
[08:55] Maya Chen: wrap — recap: Redwood to send pilot pricing spreadsheet, SOC2/KMS integration docs, runbook draft, and KV-cache + batching recommendations. Harborlytics to send usage histograms, sample prompts, and eval set. schedule 30m pilot kickoff week of 2027-02-22.
[09:13] Tom Breuer: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[09:15] Maya Chen: thanks, we'll follow up in email with attachments. bye all.
